Heaps and clustered tables in four engines
Question	PostgreSQL	MySQL (InnoDB)	SQLite	SQL Server
How is a table stored?	As a heap	Clustered by its primary key	Clustered by a hidden integer key, the rowid; WITHOUT ROWID tables by their primary key	Clustered when it has a clustered index, which a primary key creates by default; otherwise a heap
What orders a table without a primary key?	Nothing	Its first unique index on non-null columns, or else a hidden row ID	The rowid, even when another primary key is declared	Nothing, unless a clustered index is created on other columns
What does a secondary index entry carry?	A TID	The primary key columns	The rowid, or the primary key in a WITHOUT ROWID table	The clustered index key, or a row ID in a heap

Covering indexes in four engines
Question	PostgreSQL	MySQL (InnoDB)	SQLite	SQL Server
How do you add a returned column?	INCLUDE (total)	At the end of the key: (customer_id, placed_at, order_id, total)	At the end of the key	INCLUDE (total)
What does every entry cover already?	Only its key columns	The primary key, which every secondary entry carries	The rowid, which every entry carries	The clustered key, which every nonclustered entry carries
When does a covered query still visit the table?	When the page’s visibility bit is not set	When the record is marked deleted, or a newer transaction changed its index page	Never: a reader never sees the index and the table at different versions	Never

	PostgreSQL	MySQL (InnoDB)	SQLite	SQL Server
Partial index	Yes	No	Yes	Yes, called a filtered index
Expression index	Yes	Yes, called functional key parts	Yes	Through an indexed computed column
NULLs allowed in a unique index	Any number; one with NULLS NOT DISTINCT	Any number	Any number	One; a filtered unique index with WHERE email IS NOT NULL allows any number

Where each part of the history query goes in the index key
The query says	Role	In the index
customer_id = 42	Equality	First key column
placed_at >= ... and ORDER BY placed_at DESC	Range and sort on one column	Second key column, DESC to match
ORDER BY ... order_id DESC	Tie-breaker	Third key column
LIMIT 10	Early stop	Nothing, but it is why the sort order pays
SELECT ... total	Returned only	INCLUDE (total), if the query is frequent enough
status = 'paid' (the paid-only variant)	Equality, optional	After the sort columns, to check it inside the index; before them only if every query supplies it

Engine	Added to every row	Page
PostgreSQL	A 24-byte header and a 4-byte line pointer, with padding to an 8-byte boundary. A null bitmap once any column is NULL.	8 kB
InnoDB	A 5-byte header, plus a list of variable-length field sizes and NULL flags. Every clustered-index record also holds a 6-byte transaction ID and a 7-byte roll pointer to its undo, and a 6-byte row ID when the table has no primary key.	16 kB
SQL Server	A 4-byte header, a null bitmap of 2 bytes plus a bit per column, 2 bytes plus 2 more for each variable-length column, and a 2-byte slot. Up to 14 bytes more once row versioning is in use.	8 kB, 8,096 bytes of it for rows
SQLite	Two variable-length integers for the payload’s length and the rowid, a record header of one more per column, and a 2-byte cell pointer.	4 kB

Engine	When a value moves out of the row	What stays behind
PostgreSQL	Once a row passes about 2 kB, TOAST compresses its widest values and moves them into a separate table, in chunks of about 2,000 bytes, until the row is under about 2 kB.	A pointer
InnoDB	In the default DYNAMIC format, once a row passes about half a page, about 8,000 bytes, the longest variable-length columns move to overflow pages. A row that still can’t fit is refused with “Row size too large”.	A 20-byte pointer. TEXT and BLOB values of 40 bytes or less always stay.
SQL Server	A row may hold 8,060 bytes. When it grows past that, variable-length columns move to row-overflow pages, widest first. varchar(max) and similar types go to separate LOB pages when they don’t fit.	A 24-byte pointer, or 16 bytes for a LOB
SQLite	A row larger than the page less 35 bytes spills its tail onto a linked list of overflow pages.	The first part of the row

Engine	Old versions live	What a long transaction costs	One thing to look at
PostgreSQL	In the table, beside current rows	Dead versions can’t be removed, so tables and indexes grow. Rolling back is cheap, because the new versions are simply never visible.	The oldest backend_xmin in pg_stat_activity
InnoDB	In the undo log	The undo history grows. Rolling back a huge transaction can take several times as long as the change did.	History list length in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS
SQL Server, with snapshot isolation or accelerated database recovery	In the version store	The version store can’t shrink past the oldest transaction that may need it, so tempdb or the database grows.	sys.dm_tran_version_store_space_usage, or sys.dm_tran_persistent_version_store_stats with accelerated database recovery
SQLite	Nowhere in the default mode. In WAL mode, in the log.	A writer waits for readers before its final write. In WAL mode, a reader that is always open stops a checkpoint from finishing, and the log file grows without bound.	The size of the -wal file

Value	At each commit	If mysqld crashes	If the power fails or the OS crashes
1, the default	Writes the redo log and flushes it	Nothing lost	Nothing lost
2	Writes the redo log to the operating system; InnoDB flushes it about once a second, sometimes later (innodb_flush_log_at_timeout)	Nothing lost: the operating system still holds the writes	About a second of commits, sometimes more
0	Nothing; InnoDB writes and flushes the redo log on the same timer	About a second of commits, sometimes more	About a second of commits, sometimes more

Kind of data	What losing the last moments costs	A reasonable setting
Payments, orders, anything the user has seen confirmed	A confirmation that can’t be honoured, and no record to rebuild it from	The default, with full durability
Page-view and click counters	A few seconds of counts nobody will miss	Asynchronous commit, for those transactions only
Events that can be replayed from a queue or an upstream log	Replay from the source after a crash	Asynchronous commit, provided you can tell where to resume
Caches, scratch tables, test and CI databases, bulk loads that can restart	Rebuild from scratch	Unlogged tables, or flushing off for a throwaway database

Cause	How much can be lost	Database consistent afterwards?	How you would notice
Asynchronous commit	A window:
PostgreSQL: about 600 ms at the default writer delay
InnoDB at 2: about a second, after an operating-system crash
InnoDB at 0: about a second, even after a crash of the MySQL process alone
SQL Server delayed durability: whatever was still in the log buffer, after a crash or a shutdown; Microsoft states no bound
SQLite in WAL mode at NORMAL: the most recent commits
	Yes	Only by comparing with what the application remembers
A drive that acknowledges flushes it hasn’t made	No limit	Not guaranteed: in the worst case the data can be corrupted	Only by a pull-the-plug test before it happens
Flushing switched off (fsync = off, synchronous = OFF)	No limit	No: the database can be corrupt beyond repair, because the order between log and pages is no longer enforced	Errors at the next start, or none
PostgreSQL unlogged tables	All their rows after any crash	Yes: the table is empty	The table is empty after a crash or an immediate shutdown, and on a promoted standby
Failover to an asynchronous replica	The commits not yet shipped	Yes	Replication lag before the failover
Losing the disk, restoring an old backup, or committing a bad statement	Everything since the backup, or the mistake	Yes	Only a restore helps
